Time evolution was done by the Zabusky–Kruskal scheme.{{sfn | Zabusky | Kruskal | 1965}} The initial cosine wave evolves into a train of solitary-type waves.]]

The red and blue solutions show the motion of individual solitons in the absence of the other<ref>{{cite book | last=Drazin | first=P.G. | title=Solitons: an introduction | publisher=Cambridge University Press | publication-place=Cambridge; New York; Melbourne | date=1990 | isbn=0-521-33655-4}}</ref>.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''Korteweg–De Vries''' ('''KdV''') '''equation''' is a [[partial differential equation]] (PDE) which serves as a [[mathematical model]] of waves on shallow water surfaces. It is particularly notable as the prototypical example of an [[integrable system|integrable PDE]], exhibiting typical behaviors such as a large number of explicit solutions, in particular [[soliton]] solutions, and an infinite number of [[conserved quantities]], despite the nonlinearity which typically renders PDEs intractable. The KdV can be solved by the [[inverse scattering transform|inverse scattering method]] (ISM).{{sfn | Gardner | Greene | Kruskal | Miura | 1967}} In fact, [[Clifford Gardner]], [[John M. Greene]], [[Martin Kruskal]] and [[Robert Miura]] developed the classical inverse scattering method to solve the KdV equation.

The KdV equation was first introduced by  {{harvs|txt|last=Boussinesq|first=Joseph Valentin|authorlink=Joseph Valentin Boussinesq|year=1877|loc=footnote on page 360}} and rediscovered by [[Diederik Korteweg]] and [[Gustav de Vries]] in 1895, who found the simplest solution, the one-soliton solution.{{sfn | Darrigol | 2005 | p=84}}{{sfn | Korteweg | de Vries | 1895}} Understanding of the equation and behavior of solutions was greatly advanced by the computer simulations of [[Norman Zabusky]] and Kruskal in 1965 and then the development of the inverse scattering transform in 1967.

In 1972, T. Kawahara proposed a fifth-order KdV type of equation, known as [[Kawahara equation]], that describes dispersive waves, particularly in cases when the coefficient of the KdV equation becomes very small or zero.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kawahara |first=T. |title=Oscillatory solitary waves in dispersive media |journal=Journal of the Physical Society of Japan |date=1972 |volume=33 |issue=1 |pages=260–264 |doi=10.1143/JPSJ.33.260 |bibcode=1972JPSJ...33..260K }}</ref>

In 1970, a generalization of the one-dimensional Korteweg–de Vries (KdV) equation to two spatial dimensions, ''x'' and ''y'', was introduced by [[Boris Kadomtsev|Kadomtsev]] and [[Vladimir Petviashvili |Petviashvili]]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kadomtsev |first1=B. B. |last2=Petviashvili |first2=V. I. |year=1970 |title=On the stability of solitary waves in weakly dispersive media |journal=Sov. Phys. Dokl. |volume=15 |pages=539–541 |bibcode=1970SPhD...15..539K}}</ref> (see [[Kadomtsev–Petviashvili equation]]). The stability and dynamics of the KdV type solitons with respect to nonlinear transverse perturbations of finite wavelength are described by the [[Shrira-Pesenson equation]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shrira |first1=V. I. |last2=Pesenson |first2=M. Z. |year=1984 |title=Soliton stability with respect to transverse perturbations of finite length and amplitude |journal=Nonlinear and Turbulent Processes in Physics |pages=1061 |bibcode=1984ntpp.proc.1061S}}</ref>

==Definition==

The KdV equation is a [[partial differential equation]] that models (spatially) one-dimensional [[nonlinear]] [[Dispersion relation|dispersive]] [[Time_reversibility|nondissipative]] waves described by a function <math>\phi(x,t)</math> adhering to:{{sfn | Polyanin | Zaitsev | 2003|loc=Chapter 9.1.1. Korteweg-de Vries Equation}}

:<math>\partial_t \phi + \partial^3_x \phi - 6\, \phi\, \partial_x \phi =0\, \quad x \in \mathbb{R}, \; t \geq 0,</math>

where <math>\partial^3_x \phi</math> accounts for dispersion and the nonlinear element <math>\phi \partial_x \phi</math> is an [[advection]] term.

For modelling [[Shallow water equations|shallow water waves]], <math>\phi</math> is the height displacement of the water surface from its equilibrium height.

The constant <math>6</math> in front of the last term is conventional but of no great significance: multiplying <math>t</math>, <math>x</math>, and <math>\phi</math> by constants can be used to make the coefficients of any of the three terms equal to any given non-zero constants.

==Soliton solutions==

===One-soliton solution===
Consider solutions in which a fixed [[waveform]], given by <math>f(X)</math>, maintains its shape as it travels to the right at [[phase speed]] <math>c</math>.  Such a solution is given by <math>\varphi(x,t)=f(x-ct-a)=f(X)</math>. Substituting it into the KdV equation gives the [[ordinary differential equation]]

:<math>-c\frac{df}{dX}+\frac{d^3f}{dX^3}-6f\frac{df}{dX} = 0,</math>

or, integrating with respect to <math>X</math>,

:<math>-cf+\frac{d^2 f}{dX^2}-3f^2 = A </math>

where <math>A</math> is a [[constant of integration]].  Interpreting the independent variable <math>X</math> above as a virtual time variable, this means 
<math>f</math> satisfies Newton's [[equation of motion]] of a particle of unit mass in a cubic potential
:<math>V(f) = -\left(f^3+\frac{1}{2}cf^2 + Af\right)</math>.
If
:<math>A = 0,\,c > 0</math>
then the potential function <math>V(f)</math> has [[local maximum]] at <math>f=0</math>; there is a solution in which <math>f(X)</math> starts at this point at 'virtual time' 
<math>-\infty</math>, eventually slides down to the [[local minimum]], then back up the other side, reaching an equal height, and then reverses direction, ending up at the [[local maximum]] again at time <math>\infty</math>.  In other words, <math>f(X)</math> approaches <math>0</math> as <math>X\to-\infty</math>.  This is the characteristic shape of the ''[[soliton|solitary wave]]'' solution.

More precisely, the solution is

:<math>\phi(x,t)= -\frac 1 2 \, c\, \operatorname{sech}^2\left[{\sqrt{c}\over 2}(x-c\,t-a)\right]</math>

where <math>\operatorname{sech}</math> stands for the [[hyperbolic secant]] and <math>a</math> is an arbitrary constant.{{sfn | Vakakis | 2002 | pp=105-108}} This describes a right-moving [[soliton]] with velocity <math>c</math>.

=== ''N''-soliton solution ===
There is a known expression for a solution which is an <math>N</math>-soliton solution, which at late times resolves into <math>N</math> separate single solitons.{{sfn | Dunajski | 2009}} The solution depends on a set of decreasing positive parameters <math>\chi_1> \cdots> \chi_N > 0</math> and a set of non-zero parameters <math>\beta_1, \cdots, \beta_N</math>. The solution is given in the form
<math display = block> \phi(x,t) = -2\frac{\partial^2}{\partial x^2} \mathrm{log}[\mathrm{det} A(x,t)] </math>
where the components of the matrix <math>A(x,t)</math> are 
<math>A_{nm}(x,t) = \delta_{nm} + \frac{\beta_n e^{8\chi_n^3t}e^{-(\chi_n + \chi_m)x}}{\chi_n + \chi_m}.</math>

This is derived using the inverse scattering method.

==Integrals of motion==

The KdV equation has infinitely many [[integral of motion|integrals of motion]], functionals on a solution <math>\phi(t)</math> which do not change with time.{{sfn | Miura | Gardner | Kruskal | 1968}} They can be given explicitly as

:<math>\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} P_{2n-1}(\phi,\, \partial_x \phi,\, \partial_x^2 \phi,\, \ldots)\, \text{d}x\,</math>

where the polynomials <math>P_n</math> are defined recursively by
:<math>
\begin{align}
  P_1&=\phi,
  \\
  P_n &= -\frac{dP_{n-1}}{dx} + \sum_{i=1}^{n-2}\, P_i\, P_{n-1-i}
  \quad \text{ for } n \ge 2.
  \end{align}
</math>
The first few integrals of motion are:
* the mass <math>\int \phi\, \mathrm{d}x,</math>
* the momentum <math>\int \phi^2\, \mathrm{d}x,</math>
* the energy <math>\int \left[ 2 \phi^3 - \left( \partial_x \phi \right)^2 \right] \, \mathrm{d}x</math>.
Only the odd-numbered terms <math>P_{2n+1}</math> result in non-trivial (meaning non-zero) integrals of motion.{{sfn | Dingemans | 1997 | p=733}}

==Lax pairs==

The KdV equation
:<math>\partial_t\phi = 6\, \phi\, \partial_x \phi - \partial_x^3 \phi</math>
can be reformulated as the [[Lax equation]]
:<math>L_t = [L,A] \equiv LA - AL \,</math>
with <math>L</math> a [[Sturm–Liouville operator]]:
:<math>
\begin{align}
  L &= -\partial_x^2 + \phi, \\
  A &= 4 \partial_x^3 - 6 \phi\, \partial_x - 3[\partial_x, \phi]
\end{align}
</math>
where <math>[\partial_x,\phi]</math> is the [[Commutator#Identities (ring theory)|commutator]] such that <math>[\partial_x,\phi]f=f\partial_x\phi</math>.{{sfn | Polyanin | Zaitsev | 2003|loc=Chapter S.10.1. Lax Pair Method}} The Lax pair accounts for the infinite number of [[first integrals]] of the KdV equation.{{sfn | Lax | 1968}}

In fact, <math>L</math> is the time-independent [[Schrödinger operator]] (disregarding constants) with potential <math>\phi(x,t)</math>. It can be shown that due to this Lax formulation that in fact the eigenvalues do not depend on <math>t</math>.{{sfn | Dunajski | 2009|pp=31-32}}

===Zero-curvature representation===
Setting the components of the [[Lax pair#zero-curvature representation|Lax connection]] to be
<math display=block>L_x = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ \phi - \lambda & 0\end{pmatrix}, L_t = \begin{pmatrix}-\phi_x & 2\phi + 4\lambda \\ 2\phi^2 - \phi_{xx} + 2\phi\lambda - 4\lambda^2 & \phi_x\end{pmatrix},</math>
the KdV equation is equivalent to the zero-curvature equation for the Lax connection,
<math display=block>\partial_t L_x - \partial_x L_t + [L_x, L_t] = 0. </math>

==Least action principle==

The Korteweg–De Vries equation
:<math>\partial_t \phi +  6\phi\, \partial_x \phi +  \partial_x^3 \phi = 0, </math>
is the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] of motion derived from the [[Lagrangian density]], <math>\mathcal{L}\,</math>

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\mathcal{L} := \frac{1}{2} \partial_x \psi\, \partial_t \psi 
+  \left( \partial_x \psi \right)^3 
-  \frac{1}{2} \left( \partial_x^2 \psi \right)^2 </math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}

with <math>\phi</math> defined by

:<math>\phi := \frac{\partial \psi}{\partial x}. </math>

{{hidden begin|title=Derivation of Euler–Lagrange equations}}
Since the Lagrangian (eq (1)) contains second derivatives, the [[Euler–Lagrange equation]] of motion for this field is

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\partial_{\mu\mu} \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_{\mu\mu} \psi )} \right) - \partial_\mu \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_\mu \psi )} \right) + \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \psi} = 0 . </math>|{{EquationRef|2}}}}

where <math>\partial</math> is a derivative with respect to the <math>\mu</math> component.

A sum over <math>\mu</math> is implied so eq (2) really reads,

{{NumBlk|:|<math>\partial_{tt} \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_{tt} \psi )} \right) + \partial_{xx} \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_{xx} \psi )} \right) - \partial_t \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_t \psi )} \right) - \partial_x \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_x \psi )} \right) + \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \psi} = 0 .</math>|{{EquationRef|3}}}}

Evaluate the five terms of eq (3) by plugging in eq (1),

:<math>\partial_{tt} \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_{tt} \psi )} \right) = 0 </math>
:<math>\partial_{xx} \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_{xx} \psi )} \right) = \partial_{xx} \left( -\partial_{xx} \psi \right) </math>
:<math>\partial_t \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_t \psi )} \right) = \partial_t \left( \frac{1}{2} \partial_x \psi \right) </math>
:<math>\partial_x \left( \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial ( \partial_x \psi )} \right) = \partial_x \left( \frac{1}{2} \partial_t \psi + 3 (\partial_x \psi)^2 \right) \,</math>
:<math>\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \psi} = 0 </math>

Remember the definition <math>\phi = \partial_x \psi </math>, so use that to simplify the above terms,

:<math>\partial_{xx} \left( - \partial_{xx} \psi \right) = - \partial_{xxx} \phi </math>
:<math>\partial_t \left( \frac{1}{2} \partial_x \psi \right) = \frac{1}{2} \partial_t \phi </math>
:<math>\partial_x \left( \frac{1}{2} \partial_t \psi + 3 (\partial_x \psi)^2 \right) = \frac{1}{2} \partial_t \phi + 3 \partial_x (\phi)^2 = \frac{1}{2} \partial_t \phi + 6 \phi \partial_x \phi </math>

Finally, plug these three non-zero terms back into eq (3) to see
:<math>\left(- \partial_{xxx} \phi \right) - \left(\frac{1}{2} \partial_t \phi \right) - \left( \frac{1}{2} \partial_t \phi + 6 \phi \partial_x \phi \right) = 0, </math>
which is exactly the KdV equation

:<math>\partial_t \phi + 6 \phi\, \partial_x \phi + \partial_x^3 \phi = 0 .</math>
{{hidden end}}

==Long-time asymptotics==

It can be shown that any sufficiently fast decaying smooth solution will eventually split into a finite superposition of solitons travelling to the right plus a decaying dispersive part travelling to the left. This was first observed by {{harvtxt|Zabusky|Kruskal|1965}} and can be rigorously proven using the nonlinear [[Method of steepest descent|steepest descent]] analysis for oscillatory [[Riemann–Hilbert problem]]s.{{sfn|Grunert|Teschl|2009}}

==History==

The history of the KdV equation  started with experiments by [[John Scott Russell]] in 1834, followed by theoretical investigations by [[Lord Rayleigh]] and [[Joseph Boussinesq]] around 1870 and, finally, Korteweg and De Vries in 1895.

The KdV equation was not studied much after this until {{harvtxt|Zabusky|Kruskal|1965}} discovered numerically that its solutions seemed to decompose at large times into a collection of "solitons": well separated  solitary waves. Moreover, the solitons seems to be almost unaffected in shape by passing through each other (though this could cause a change in their position).  They also made the connection to earlier numerical experiments by [[Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou problem|Fermi, Pasta, Ulam, and Tsingou]] by showing that the KdV equation was the [[continuum limit]] of the [[Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou problem|FPUT]] system.  Development of the analytic solution by means of the [[inverse scattering transform]] was done in 1967 by Gardner, Greene, Kruskal and Miura.{{sfn | Gardner | Greene | Kruskal | Miura | 1967}}{{sfn | Dauxois | Peyrard | 2006}}

The KdV equation is now seen to be closely connected to [[Huygens' principle]].{{sfn | Chalub | Zubelli | 2006}}{{sfn | Berest | Loutsenko | 1997}}

==Applications and connections==

The KdV equation has several connections to physical problems.  In addition to being the governing equation of the string in the [[Fermi–Pasta–Ulam–Tsingou problem]] in the continuum limit, it approximately describes the evolution of long, one-dimensional waves in many physical settings, including:
* shallow-water waves with weakly [[non-linear]] restoring forces,
* long [[internal wave]]s in a density-stratified [[ocean]],
* [[ion acoustic wave]]s in a [[plasma (physics)|plasma]],
* [[Acoustics|acoustic]] waves on a [[crystal lattice]].

The KdV equation can also be solved using the inverse scattering transform similarly to the [[non-linear Schrödinger equation]].

===KdV equation and the Gross–Pitaevskii equation ===
{{Unreferenced section|date=September 2015}}

Considering the simplified solutions of the form
:<math>\phi(x,t)=\phi(x \pm t) </math>
we obtain the KdV equation as
:<math> \pm \partial_x \phi + \partial^3_x \phi + 6\, \phi\, \partial_x \phi =0\,</math>
or
:<math> \pm \partial_x \phi +  \partial_x (\partial^2_x \phi + 3 \phi^2) =0\,</math>
Integrating and taking the special case in which the integration constant is zero, we have:
:<math>  -\partial^2_x \phi - 3 \phi^2 =\pm \phi \,</math>
which is the <math>\lambda=1</math> special case of the generalized stationary [[Gross–Pitaevskii equation]] (GPE)
:<math>  -\partial^2_x \phi - 3 \phi^{\lambda} \phi =\pm \phi \,</math>
Therefore, for the certain class of solutions of generalized GPE (<math>\lambda=4</math> for the true one-dimensional condensate and
<math>\lambda=2</math> while using the three dimensional equation in one dimension), two equations are one. Furthermore, taking the <math>\lambda=3</math> case with the minus sign and the <math>\phi</math> real, one obtains an attractive self-interaction that should yield a [[bright soliton]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Pitaevskii |first=Lev |author-link=Lev Pitaevskii |title=Vortex Lines in an Imperfect Bose Gas |url=https://jetp.ras.ru/cgi-bin/dn/e_013_02_0451.pdf |journal=[[Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Physics]] |volume=13 |issue=2 |pages=451-454}}</ref>
